newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai exports remain weak but C/A deficit narrows.
newsitem.headline: Thai exports remain weak but C/A deficit narrows.

text.p: Thailand's cental bank on Thursday released key economic indicators showing sustained weak exports but an improving trend in the country's current account deficit.

Bank of Thailand (BOT) economist Suchada Kirakul told reporters that the bank revised the July trade deficit to 35.3 billion baht ($1.4 billion) from 30.0 billion estimated earlier for the month. The deficit in June was 36.9 billion.
Thai exports rose a marginal 2.9 percent year-on-year during January-July against hefty 26.5 percent growth seen in the same period a year ago.

Suchada said July exports were adjusted down to 110.8 billion baht from 118.0 billion estimated earlier, and against 109.1 billion in June. The July figure was 1.2 percent lower than a year ago, the second monthly decline in a row after a steep 9.8 percent fall in June.
However, she noted that the Thai current account deficit narrowed for the third straight month to about 30.8 billion baht in July from 35.4 billion in June, partly due to an import slowdown.

"The figures look all very bearish," said Chatchai Saelee of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities. "I can't see Thailand meeting its 10.2 percent export growth target this year. The maximum growth we could achieve is probably seven to eight percent."

He said August bank credit and investment figures also confirmed a sustained weakening trend of the Thai economy that would likely grow at a pace substantially lower than the 7.8 percent targeted by the central bank for this year.
"I would put the 1996 Gross Domestic Product growth at about 7.0 percent," Chatchai said.
Central bank officials have said the sluggish exports reflected a regional phenomenon brought about by sluggish consumer spending in the major U.S. and European markets.
Suchada said Thai shipments of computer circuit boards and electronic parts rose a slow nine percent year-on-year in July against over a 30 percent increase in the first quarter of 1996.

July industrial exports fell 1.5 percent year-on-year after an 8.8 percent decline the previous month. Shipment of manufactured goods increased only 4.6 percent in the first seven months of 1996, against 21.3 percent growth a year ago.

She said foreign market speculation against the baht on devaluation rumours in late July and early August triggered a net capital outflow in the first half of August, but the situation was reversed in the second half.

The economist said the Thai balance of payments swung back to an estimated 2.6 billion baht surplus in August from a rare 17.1 billion baht deficit seen in July when the baht was attacked by foreign speculators.
She said Thailand's August capital account posted a slightly higher net inflow than the 5.3 billion baht posted in July.

The economist said Thai foreign reserves, used by the central bank to defend the baht in local and regional markets, stood unchanged at end-August from the $39.4 billion of the previous month, but against $39.8 billion at end-June.
The steady foreign reserve figure puzzled some market analysts who had expected it to fall to about $38.5 billion.
